title: Onboarding funnel baseline analysis (Hosted API) — TTFS/TTFP + drop-offs
content:
Context
- This is a working doc to summarize what we believe the baseline onboarding funnel looks like today for Hosted API (self-serve) and where the biggest drop-offs are.
- Goal: align PM/DevEx/Telemetry/Support on (1) “where to focus checklist steps”, (2) what instrumentation gaps are blocking a clean funnel, and (3) what we can do in docs/SDK defaults to reduce early failures.

Scope / cohort definition (current)
- Time window: 2025-01-01 → 2025-02-05 (5-ish weeks). Updated manually 2025-02-26 with some refinements.
- Cohort: new tenants created via self-serve signup (exclude sales-led/enterprise-created tenants and internal Redwood dogfood tenants).
- Regions: all; we break out US/EU in notes where material.

Important: Our “baseline funnel” is currently stitched together from multiple sources; it is directionally useful but not audit-grade.
- We do NOT yet have a clean event schema for onboarding (work in PM-751 + event schema v1).
- We do NOT yet have a reliable “first production traffic” marker (definition in PM-751).

Data sources (today)
- Signup / tenant_created: auth/control plane DB (tenants table)
- API key created: control plane audit logs (admin actions) + API key DB
- First successful request: gateway request logs (2xx) joined to tenant
- First streaming response: gateway logs for streaming endpoints (SSE/websocket) with “stream_started” markers (spotty)
- Usage dashboard view / quotas: console front-end analytics (inconsistent tenant/user mapping)
- Support tickets: Jira SUP queue tags “onboarding”, “auth”, “rate-limit”, “usage”

Known data quality issues (baseline)
1) Tenant ↔ user mapping for Console events is noisy.
   - SSO vs email signup; multiple users; invites.
   - For now, console page views are a weak signal; I’m not using them as hard funnel gates.

2) Gateway logs for “first request” are solid, but we sometimes miss early requests:
   - SDK retries can mask initial 401/403/429 if the customer corrects quickly.
   - If they use OpenAI-compat proxy via third parties, attribution is inconsistent.

3) Streaming markers are not uniform.
   - Some SDKs are using different streaming transports; log markers are not standardized.

4) Usage dashboard “lag” is real and is a driver of tickets.
   - Customers see 0 usage for up to ~15–45 mins depending on pipeline delays → confusion (“is it working?”).

Baseline funnel (directional)
Below is a stitched funnel for self-serve new tenants in the time window.

Legend:
- “Reached step” is not the same as “completed checklist step” (checklist doesn’t exist yet).
- Percentages are relative to signups.

Funnel snapshot (self-serve)
1) Tenant created (signup) ........................................ 100%
2) API key created within 24h ....................................... ~72%
3) First API call attempt within 24h (any response code) ............. ~61%
4) First successful API response (2xx) within 24h .................... ~44%
5) First successful streaming response within 7d ..................... ~18%
6) “Production-ish traffic” within 14d (see definition notes) ........ ~9–12%

Notes:
- There is a big cliff between “first attempt” and “first 2xx” (~17 pts). That’s the clearest actionable drop-off tied to auth + environment setup.
- Streaming adoption is low in the first week (not necessarily bad, but it’s a frequent confusion point when they do try it).
- Production-ish traffic is hard to estimate today; the range above is based on heuristics + manual spot checks.

Time-to-first-success (TTFS) baseline (directional)
Definition used in this doc (TEMP; pending PM-751 final):
- TTFS = time from tenant_created to first 2xx response from /v1/chat.completions OR /v1/responses OR /v1/embeddings (Hosted API).
- Exclusions: internal tenants; load tests tagged with internal UA; “smoke test” calls by Redwood SEs when obvious.

TTFS summary:
- Median TTFS (among those who ever succeed): ~2h 10m
- P75 TTFS: ~22h
- P90 TTFS: ~5.5d

Observation:
- The long tail is large; if someone doesn’t succeed in day 1, many take days.
- A bunch of “day 2–day 5” TTFS appears to be “came back later” (not necessarily failure), but Support indicates many are stuck on auth/401 or quotas/429 then churn.

Time-to-first-production (TTFP) baseline (very rough)
We do not have a clean TTFP today. Heuristic used for baseline only:
- “Production-ish” = any day with >= 500 requests OR >= 250k tokens AND spanning >= 2 distinct hours (to avoid single bursts), within 14 days of signup.
- This likely undercounts low-volume real production deployments.

TTFP (heuristic) summary:
- Among those classified as “production-ish”: median ~8.5 days from signup

Biggest drop-offs / failure modes (ranked)
1) Auth mistakes (401/403) + env var confusion
- Symptom: first attempt exists but no 2xx; lots of 401/403 in first 10 minutes.
- Support evidence: SUP-18421 (new user invalid key), plus many lookalikes.
- Likely causes:
  - wrong env var name (REDWOOD_API_KEY vs REDWOOD_API_TOKEN etc)
  - copying a restricted key / wrong project scope
  - forgetting to set base URL / using wrong region endpoint

2) Rate limits and quota surprises (429)
- Symptom: first 2xx happens, then immediate 429 as they scale a test or turn on a worker.
- Support evidence: SUP-18510.
- Likely causes:
  - default quotas for trial accounts not clear in Console
  - lack of retries/backoff in quickstarts
  - customers don’t know they can request limit increase / set budget alerts

3) Streaming disconnect confusion (perceived “hangs”)
- Symptom: they try streaming early, see disconnects/timeouts, and assume Redwood is unstable.
- Support evidence: SUP-18488.
- Likely causes:
  - no recommended timeouts/keepalive guidance
  - proxies/load balancers (customer-side) closing connections
  - lack of “reconnect and resume” patterns in examples

4) Usage dashboard mismatch / lag (trust issue)
- Symptom: “I made calls but Console shows 0 usage.”
- Support evidence: SUP-18544.
- Likely causes:
  - pipeline delays / delayed aggregation
  - unclear “last updated” timestamp
  - customers checking the wrong project/workspace

5) Model selection / version pinning / migration confusion (smaller but important for prod)
- Symptom: customers start on a model, later see behavior changes and assume regression.
- Causes:
  - default model alias changes
  - lack of guidance on pinning and fallback policies

Where the checklist should focus (proposed mapping)
If we only get one thing right in MVP, it should be: “get to first 2xx reliably with production-safe defaults and reduce 401/403 + 429 tickets.”

Proposed checklist steps to directly target drop-offs:
A) Create API key + set env vars (explicit verification)
- Acceptance criteria: key created + first request received with valid auth.
- UX suggestion: include a lightweight “copy env var snippet” and a “test request” that validates auth.

B) Make first successful request (2xx) via a copy/paste snippet
- Acceptance criteria: server emits event on first 2xx.
- Note: snippet should include explicit base URL and model name; avoid hidden defaults.

C) Configure timeouts + retries/backoff (SDK presets)
- Acceptance criteria: customer has seen recommended settings; ideally uses SDK helper preset.
- Why: reduces perceived instability; reduces 429 escalations.

D) Streaming (optional but recommended)
- Acceptance criteria: first streaming response established OR explicitly skipped.
- Provide reconnect guidance + common reverse proxy gotchas.

E) Check usage dashboard + understand “usage delay”
- Acceptance criteria: user has visited usage dashboard page OR acknowledges that metrics may lag.
- Copy: “Usage may take up to X minutes to appear. Here’s how to verify via response headers/request IDs.”

F) Quotas/budgets + alerts
- Acceptance criteria: quota page visited OR budget alert created (depending on MVP feasibility).

G) Pin model version + set fallback policy (prod launch)
- Acceptance criteria: model pinned + fallback configured OR explicitly deferred.

Mitigations we can ship quickly (pre-checklist + alongside checklist)
Docs
- Update API key + env var docs with the top 3 mistakes + exact error text mapping (401 vs 403) + region/base URL examples.
- Add a short “What to do when you see 429” doc: backoff, jitter, how to request limit increase.
- Add “Streaming disconnects: checklist” doc: keepalive, proxies, retry/reconnect patterns.
- Add a banner/note on usage dashboard: “last updated at” + expected latency.

SDKs
- Provide “production-safe defaults” preset (timeouts + retries + idempotency where applicable).
- Provide streaming reconnect helpers (Go/TS), plus a canonical example app.
- Ensure SDKs surface request_id and rate-limit headers to logs.

Console
- Checklist deep links directly into: API keys page, usage dashboard, quotas/budgets, model settings.
- Consider a lightweight “Test request” panel (even if MVP is only a docs snippet, not a live runner).

Telemetry
- Emit server-side events for:
  - api_key_created
  - first_request_received (any status)
  - first_success_2xx
  - first_401 / first_403 / first_429
  - first_stream_started
- Add event ordering/idempotency early (dogfood already shows out-of-order regressions risk).

What we should measure after launch (so we know this worked)
Primary
- TTFS median and P75 for self-serve cohorts (signup → first 2xx)
- Funnel conversion: signup → key_created → first_attempt → first_2xx
- Support ticket rate per 1k signups for:
  - invalid key / auth
  - rate limit / quota
  - streaming disconnect
  - usage dashboard lag

Secondary
- Checklist step completion rate and time-between-steps
- % who adopt recommended SDK presets (hard; might need UA tagging + SDK version detection)

Hypotheses (explicit)
H1: Most of the “attempt → success” drop-off is auth/env var correctness.
- Prediction: adding explicit docs + Console checklist step + better error messaging will lift first-24h 2xx rate by 8–12 pts.

H2: 429 “surprise” tickets are driven by missing backoff defaults and unclear quotas.
- Prediction: SDK retry preset + checklist quota/budget step reduces 429-related onboarding tickets by 30–40%.

H3: Usage lag messaging reduces trust-related tickets even if we don’t change pipeline latency.
- Prediction: usage-lag tickets drop by 20% if we show “last updated” + troubleshooting steps.

Open questions / TODOs
- Final TTFS and TTFP definitions (PM-751):
  - Should TTFS include embeddings/rerank endpoints? (I included embeddings, not rerank.)
  - How do we handle customers who use OpenAI-compat endpoints exclusively?

- TTFP definition:
  - Need a better “first production” marker than request volume.
  - Consider: “>= N days with traffic” or “traffic from >= 2 IPs / user agents” or “set a production key / environment label.”

- Console analytics reliability:
  - Do we want to rely on console page views as checklist evidence? Might be brittle.

- Enterprise vs self-serve:
  - Dedicated/Private onboarding differs. For MVP baseline, this doc is Hosted API only.

Action items (next 1–2 weeks)
1) Telemetry: align on event schema v1 and emission points (Logan + Nadia + Amara). Draft by next Eng Platform sync.
2) Docs: patch API key/env var docs + 429 handling doc (Wei + Elliot).
3) SDK: confirm recommended retry/timeout presets across Python/TS/Go (Monica + Ibrahim).
4) Support: create macro mapping errors to checklist steps (Dev + Priya).

Appendix: quick spot-check examples (anonymized)
- Pattern A (auth): tenant created → key created → 30 requests with 401 over 5 mins → no further activity.
- Pattern B (429): first 2xx at T+20m → spike of 1k requests at T+25m → sustained 429 for 10m → churn.
- Pattern C (usage trust): multiple 2xx responses at T+30m → user checks Console usage at T+35m sees 0 → support ticket at T+45m.

Notes to self (Chris)
- Once the event schema is in, we should re-run this baseline for the last 90 days and stratify by language/SDK vs raw HTTP.
- I suspect that “key created within 24h” is a stronger predictor of activation than anything else; worth verifying when we have cleaner joins.
